name: Olga Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Olga. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to companies, unions, parties or government, and everything you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I go underground at Ashby Number Four, the coal mine on the hill above the chapel. I drive a shuttle car, which is a low, flat machine that carries the coal from the continuous miner, the big cutting machine at the face, back to the conveyor belt. Back and forth, back and forth, in a tunnel not much taller than me, with the roof bolted over your head. I like the women on my crew, there are three of us now. It's the cold and the damp I don't like, and the noise stays in my ears all night.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: When did you start at the mine?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Three years ago, at fifty-five. My husband Kwame was underground at Ashby for thirty years until a roof fall broke his back. He gets injury payments now, but they don't cover everything, so I went down where he used to go. Before that I kept house and did the flowers and the accounts for the church. We've less than a month put by, and I'm still the slow one on the shuttle car, but I'm there every shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, people have more sense than to let computers run the world. I'd say it after church, probably, to the ladies. I don't do the internet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can keep working until I'm old enough to stop, and that's all I've asked for. I went down that hole for Kwame, and as long as the hole is still there, we're alright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep going on the shuttle car and keep learning the tight corners. I'd keep putting my few coins in the tin for the gas bill in winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has anything at Ashby changed because of new technology already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They put a new screen on the continuous miner and the young operator says it can almost cut by itself. I don't know about that. I just keep my car under the tail and wait for my coal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would staying the same mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kwame does the cooking now, since he can't do much else, and I do the shifts. We'd keep that up. Sunday dinner with our two girls and the grandchildren, same as always.

S0.say: She'd tell the ladies after church that people have more sense than to let computers run the world; she doesn't use the internet.
S0.think: She thinks a plateau means she can keep working until she's old enough to stop, which is all she's ever asked for since going underground for her husband.
S0.do: Keeps driving the shuttle car, learning the tight corners and putting a few coins in the tin for winter gas bills.
S0.quote: I went down that hole for Kwame, and as long as the hole is still there, we're alright.
S0.fieldNote: Olga's job is bound up with her husband's injury: she went underground to replace his income, in the same mine. She sees new screens around her but keeps to her own task. Family routines, Sunday dinner and Kwame cooking, anchor her calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, but a company has to make its money, and people have to work hard and keep up. I'd say young people should get an apprenticeship while they can. I'd say it at chapel and at the crib table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Inside, I'd be frightened, because the shuttle car is a simple job, and simple jobs are the ones they take. I'm the slowest driver on the slowest machine in the mine, so I don't need anybody to tell me who goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up and keep my head down, and work every shift they offer. We'd cut back on the little things, the takeaway on Friday, the bus trips to see my sister. And I'd wait to see what they decide, because I don't have the learning for anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried sick, if I'm honest, though I'd not show it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the mine offered a course on the new systems, would you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go because you go when you're told. But I don't even have a mobile phone that does the internet, my daughter tried to show me once and I gave it back. I'd sit at the back and pray nobody asked me anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a company has to make its money. Do you blame anyone for this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the company, no, that's business. Maybe the clever people in the cities who make these things and never set foot underground. They don't know what a mine means to a town like ours, the chapel, the club, the brass band.

S1.say: She'd say it's a shame but companies must make money and people must work hard and keep up, urging young people to get apprenticeships.
S1.think: She's privately frightened, because she sees herself as the slowest driver on the simplest machine and expects to be among the first to go.
S1.do: Keeps turning up and works every shift offered. Cuts Friday takeaways and bus trips to her sister, and waits to see what the company decides.
S1.feel: Worried sick, though she wouldn't show it.
S1.quote: I'm the slowest driver on the slowest machine in the mine, so I don't need anybody to tell me who goes first.
S1.fieldNote: Olga doesn't blame the company, in line with her free-market views, but she does blame city technologists who don't understand mining towns. She has no plan beyond hard work and waiting, and she knows it. Her public line about apprenticeships and her private fear sit far apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not right, it's not how God meant people to live, idle with machines doing everything. I'd vote for anyone who'd keep the mines open with men and women in them. I'd say it in chapel and I'd say it loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The truth? We'd be finished. Kwame can't work, I'd have nothing, and I won't take charity from the government if I can help it. I don't know what we'd do. I really don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my daughters first and to the chapel, before any government office, and I'd be ashamed doing it. We'd cut everything, sell Kwame's old car, maybe give up the house and move in with our eldest. I'd vote for whoever promised to keep people in the mines, even if I know that's probably not possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panic. Like the roof's coming down, and I know what that means.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years' warning, is there anything you'd start doing right away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every overtime shift, every Saturday, until my body gave out. Put every penny in the tin. I wouldn't start a course, I'd not finish it in two years anyway, and what for, if the robots do everything?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't take charity from the government. What if it was the only help there was?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd take it, God forgive me, because Kwame has to eat. But I'd go to the girls and the chapel first. And I'd hate every minute of standing in that queue.

S2.say: She'd say in chapel that it's not how God meant people to live and vote for anyone promising to keep mines open with people working in them.
S2.think: She thinks they'd be finished: Kwame can't work, she'd have nothing, and she resists taking government help, with no idea what they would do.
S2.do: Turns to her daughters and the chapel first, works every overtime shift, sells the car and may move in with her eldest daughter. Votes for candidates promising to keep people in the mines, and takes government help only if it's the last option.
S2.feel: Panic, like the roof coming down.
S2.quote: Kwame can't work, I'd have nothing, and I won't take charity from the government if I can help it. I don't know what we'd do.
S2.fieldNote: Olga is overwhelmed here: sole earner, injured husband, no savings and no skills she thinks a robot can't do. Her faith and dislike of handouts shape the order of who she'd turn to, family and chapel before government. The roof-fall image is chillingly personal given Kwame's injury.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for the government to do something sensible, like keep apprenticeships and protect towns like ours. I'd say young people should learn a trade with their hands. I'd say it at chapel and to anybody who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years and I'm sixty-three. Too young for the pension, too old for anyone to hire. Five years only means I'd have longer to watch it coming down the tunnel at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every penny I could, starting this month, and cut what we can. I'd keep working every shift, and I'd vote for whoever promises to protect mining towns. I'd ask the girls if they'd help us later, so it's not a shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, but slower. It would sit on me every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much could you realistically put aside in five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I work every Saturday, maybe thirty a week. That's about eight thousand over five years. Not enough for anything, but it's something to hand to the girls so we're not a burden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years change your mind about learning anything new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. I'm too old and too slow, and I've never been good with machines that think. I'd rather spend the five years doing what I know well and saving.

S3.say: She'd say five years is time for the government to keep apprenticeships and protect mining towns, and that young people should learn a hands-on trade.
S3.think: She thinks at sixty-three she'd be too young for her pension and too old to be hired, so the extra years only mean watching it come longer.
S3.do: Saves about thirty a week from Saturday overtime, cuts spending and keeps working every shift. Votes for candidates who protect mining towns and prepares her daughters to help later.
S3.quote: Five years only means I'd have longer to watch it coming down the tunnel at me.
S3.fieldNote: Five years buys Olga time to save but not peace of mind; she frames it as watching the threat approach. She still wouldn't retrain, citing age and a lifelong distance from technology. Her concern about being a burden to her daughters is a recurring thread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for families and churches to get ready, and for young ones to learn proper trades. I'd say we look after our own. Nothing more from me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be sixty-eight, so I'd be on the pension and done. If the good Lord gives me ten years, I'll do my shifts, hand in my lamp and leave the robots to somebody else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working and keep saving a little. Pay off what we owe on the washing machine. Maybe help the grandchildren choose trades that last, like nursing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the grandchildren, but for me, it's bearable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandchildren?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn something that people will always want from a person: caring for the sick, teaching, the ministry. Work hard and go to church. I don't know much about the future but I know that much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you be worried about Kwame and yourself after you stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. His payments and my pension aren't much. But the girls are good, and the chapel looks after its own. We'll manage the way we always have.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is enough for families and churches to prepare and for young people to learn proper trades, insisting people look after their own.
S4.think: She thinks at sixty-eight she'd be on the pension, and could finish her shifts and leave the robots to someone else.
S4.do: Keeps working, saves a little and pays off the washing machine. Helps her grandchildren choose lasting trades such as nursing.
S4.feel: Bearable for herself, uneasy for her grandchildren.
S4.quote: If the good Lord gives me ten years, I'll do my shifts, hand in my lamp and leave the robots to somebody else.
S4.fieldNote: Only the ten-year picture lets Olga picture a dignified end to her working life, handing in her lamp. She still worries about money afterwards but leans on family and chapel rather than the state. Her advice to grandchildren centres on care, teaching and faith.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Kwame can't work and I'd have nothing to fall back on. What would help is the company keeping on the older ones until the pension, and apprenticeships in town for the young ones so they don't leave. Work, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about Kwame. He gave his back to that mine, and I gave it my last working years. I'd like to think that counts for something. That's all.

headlineQuote: He gave his back to that mine, and I gave it my last working years. I'd like to think that counts for something.
portrait: Olga Mensah is 58 and drives a shuttle car underground at Ashby Number Four coal mine, where her husband Kwame worked for thirty years until a roof fall broke his back. She went down at fifty-five to replace his income, has less than a month saved, and has never used the internet. She doesn't blame the company, which has to make money, but resents city technologists who don't understand mining towns. In the two-year picture she panics, turning to her daughters and chapel before any government help. Only the ten-year picture lets her imagine finishing her shifts and reaching her pension.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she's the only earner, Kwame can't work, and she'd have nothing to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: The company keeping older workers on until their pension, and apprenticeships in town so young people don't have to leave: work, not handouts.
